title: To God we return
hookLine: Muslims say "to God we belong and to God we return" on hearing of a loss
carry: who could be better than him
last: PATIENCE IS AT THE FIRST STROKE.

lines: A MESSAGE: HER GRANDMOTHER HAS DIED.
THE SAME SENTENCE, OVER AND OVER.
cards: The phone lights up with a message from a Muslim friend: her grandmother has died. The replies begin with the same Arabic phrase, or its initials: inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un.
Different people, different spellings, the same sentence. Muslims say it on hearing of a death, and of other losses too. It isn't a condolence card.
It's a verse, and it comes from yesterday's passage.

teach.h: THE STEADFAST ARE KNOWN BY WHAT THEY SAY.
teach.b: First, where it comes from. Yesterday's verses gave good news to the steadfast.

teach.h: WE ARE GOD'S. WE ARE RETURNING.
teach.b: The next verse describes them: they are those "Who say, when a misfortune striketh them: Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning." That's Pickthall's English. The patient are known by what they say.
Second, two halves. We are God's: in this reading, whatever was lost was never simply owned. Not the money, not the health, not even the people we love.
Unto Him we are returning: the one who has died has gone back where everyone is going. The sentence holds the loss and the hope in one breath. Third, a widow's story.

In the hadith collection of Muslim, Umm Salama tells how the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, taught that someone struck by a loss should say this verse, and ask God for reward in the affliction and something better in its place.
When her husband Abu Salama died, she said it, and wondered who could be better than him. Later the Prophet himself asked to marry her. She said it before she could imagine any answer.

teach.h: A WEEK OF WORDS FOR SUFFERING.
teach.b: Fourth, looking back on a week of suffering. Two grieving sisters, and Jesus weeping with them. A wish, said plainly in a garden.
A thorn that stayed. Ease, promised twice. Patience at the first stroke.
And now a sentence for the moment the news arrives. Again and again, the texts give people words for the worst moment, and leave the why unanswered.

how: Muslims say inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un on hearing of a death or another loss, and write it in messages of condolence.

o: a widow who said the verse when her husband died
the first woman to memorize the whole Quran
the Prophet's daughter, who led the early prayers

games.q: you're Umm Salama. your husband has died, and you've been taught to ask God for something better in his place. you can't imagine anyone better. what do you do?
o: wait until you feel it's true.
games.why: she says it, wondering who could be better than Abu Salama. later the Prophet asks to marry her.

practice: Think of something you once called yours and no longer have, a person, a home, a job, the body you had at twenty, and name it silently.
Try the verse's shape in your own words, if it fits: where it came from, then where it has gone; or simply, it was given, it is gone, it mattered.
If you're Muslim, or if you wish, you can say the verse itself, then let the loss stay a while in the quiet after.

wordCard.voice: Umm Salama, the widow in the hadith who said this verse on losing her husband, and whom the Prophet later asked to marry. Today's word.
